newsitem.title: UK: Britain seeks to ease N.Irish parades tension.
newsitem.headline: Britain seeks to ease N.Irish parades tension.

text.p: Britain tried to ease alarm about Northern Ireland's "marching season" on Tuesday, claiming Protestants and Catholics might yet thrash out a compromise ahead of a flashpoint pro-British parade on Sunday.

Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam met new Irish Prime Minister Bertie Ahern for the first time since he took power last week to discuss her attempts to broker a deal between the parade organisers and local Catholics who plan a counter event.

"We still have four or five days, we are still meeting and talking with the residents' groups. I don't accept yet that an accommodation is not possible because then you get people entrenching and you get the situation building up to the kind of problems that we faced last year," Mowlam told reporters.
Last year police stopped the annual Orange Order parade in Portadown but relented after four days of Protestant riots and road blockades.
Minority Catholics reacted furiously accusing Britain of caving into mob rule and Catholic gangs clashed viciously with riot police for several days.
"I have said it clearly that we are still trying to get an accommodation, and that is what we will work for," Mowlam said before attending a trade union conference with Ahern.

"We'll be working closely with the Secretary of State (Mowlam) to try to make sure that her excellent efforts over recent weeks to try to find an accommodation that is suitable to everybody can work," Ahern said. He meets British Prime Minister Tony Blair on Thursday.
Many in the province fear that if Sunday's parade in Portadown spills over into violence, views will harden on all sides and make more difficult the quest for a fresh IRA ceasefire.
The murder last month of two policemen by the IRA severely tested the patience of pro-British Loyalist militias who announced a ceasefire in October 1994.

Security analysts say Mowlam and police chiefs will soon have to decide whether to ban one or other of the Portadown demonstrations. Catholics said last week they would hold "a street festival" in the path of the Orange march.
Mowlam signalled it was not yet time to decide on a possible ban and British sources said that a compromise might still be possble.
The march's flashpoint area is the three-quarter mile (one km) long Garvaghy Road, a Catholic enclave of sprawling estates in the largely Protestant town in County Armagh, near the Irish border.
Catholics residents' leaders announced plans on Tuesday for "peace camps" and a roadside picket by local women along Garvaghy Road starting on Wednesday night.
The Orange Order holds hundreds of summer marches in the province that climax on July 12, the anniversary of a 1690 Protestant battlefield victory over the Catholic Irish.
It says it has made concessions over parades in Portadown in recent years but that Catholics are fired by anti-Britishness and intolerance of the Protestants' traditions.
Catholics are angry that the Orange Order has refused to meet them for face-to-face discussions and say Orange parades are intended to make them feel second-class citizens.
